recordings.text: A fork, and a clean one. A lone attacker bears on several targets, and the defense must deal with every one of them.
A costly lapse. A fork is handed over: one enemy piece will bear on several targets. Find the square where that piece lands.
A fork was there to be taken, a lone attacker bearing on several targets. That chance was left lying. Go back and find the square.
That is a proper pin. The piece in front of its king cannot step off the line, because doing so would expose the king behind it.
A real concession. Now the other side can pin a piece against its king and hold it to that line.
The stronger move was a pin against the king. The pinned piece would have been chained in place, since stepping off exposes its king. That chance goes begging.
A skewer, well aimed. Hit the front piece; once it gives way, the one behind it is open to capture.
This leaves two pieces on one line for the other side to skewer. Shift the front piece, and whatever stands behind it may be laid open.
The stronger move was a skewer. The attack would have gone through the front piece to the one behind it. That chance is wasted here.
This is the right target. Take the defender, and everything it protected is left bare.
A defender is now within the other side's reach. If it falls, the pieces it guards lose their cover. Know which pieces depend on it.
The defender was the target, and another move could have captured it. Whatever it guarded would have lost its protection. Here the defender survives untouched, and that is a lost opportunity.
A back-rank strike, and a sharp one. The king is a prisoner of its own pieces on the back rank.
The back rank is weak, and this move lets the other side use it. The king's own pieces block its escape, and that is a route to mate.
The king was sealed in by its own pieces, and a back-rank mate was ready. It goes unplayed. A finish like that should not be missed.
The pawn is on course for the last rank, and the aim is to promote it. Follow that road square by square.
This opens the promotion road for the other side. A pawn of theirs is free to march for the last rank. Stop pawns like that early.
The stronger move would have sent a pawn clear through to promotion. This move ignores that road.
A discovered attack, and a forceful one. Unmasked: the piece in front moves, and the attacker behind it is free. Clear the line, and the hidden piece does the work.
One of their pieces stands in front of another, and this move lets the screen lift. When it steps aside, the piece behind is free to attack.
The stronger move uncovered an attack; shift the front piece, and the hidden attacker would have struck. This move keeps that threat hidden.
Double attack. That is forcing play, and the defense has to answer both threats at once.
This lets the other side attack twice with a single move. One move of theirs creates two threats, and a single reply has to meet both.
The stronger move was a double attack. This move lets that double attack go to waste.
Deflection, executed well. With its defender hauled away, the guarded point falls open.
A defender carries a vital task, and the other side can now drag it away. That is a deflection, and the task would go uncovered.
A stronger move could have dragged a defender away from its post. That deflection was the better idea, and here it is wasted.
A piece stood without a guard, and the move takes it. A loose piece is an invitation; this move accepts it.
The stronger move simply took an undefended piece. Nothing guarded it. Loose pieces must be checked before every move.
A piece is left hanging, and the other side can take it for free. Every piece must be accounted for before a move is made.
Careless with protection: the move strips a piece of its only real defender. What it was guarding can now be captured. A defender's duty must be known before it moves.
The opponent's last move threatened something, and this move ignores it. Now a piece can be taken for free. Every move must answer the one before it.
This trade loses value. The first capture looks fine, but the recapture takes back more than was won. Never stop counting an exchange halfway.
Development: a minor piece is out and in the fight. A piece left at home does no work.
A different move would have developed a minor piece off its home square.
Rook to an open file, where no pawn of either color stands. That is where a rook belongs.
An open file was there for a rook with a different move, a file stripped of every pawn.
A good file for the rook: semi-open. Its own pawns are off it, and an enemy pawn remains there to press against.
A semi-open file was available for a rook with a different move: clear of friendly pawns, with an enemy pawn as a target.
Now there is a passed pawn on the board. Its file and both neighboring files ahead of it are free of enemy pawns. Passed pawns must be pushed or stopped.
With a different move, a pawn would have been passed: its path and both neighboring files free of enemy pawns.
The passed pawn gains another rank. It was already free; now it is closer to the last rank and harder to ignore.
A different move would have advanced the passed pawn a step nearer promotion.
The move leaves a pawn isolated. With no friendly pawn on the files either side, only pieces can defend it.
A different move would have left a pawn cut off from friendly pawns on both neighboring files, an isolated pawn.
A lone piece now has a guard. Protected pieces are hard targets.
Another move would have given an undefended piece the protection it lacked.
This piece now stands without a defender. That does not yet make it a loss, but it is now a target to watch.
With a different move, one piece would have ended up undefended. Note the weakness, but do not call it a loss.
The king now has a legal square to run to. An escape square is worth having.
A different move would have given the king a legal square to escape to.
Castling: the king tucks in and the rook crosses over. Both pieces move in a single turn.
Castling was the alternative, moving king and rook in a single move.
This capture costs a side its bishop pair. It no longer has a bishop for each color of square.
A different move would have captured a bishop and stripped the other side of the bishop pair.
Doubled pawns now, one stacked in front of the other on a single file. They cannot protect each other.
A different move would have stacked two pawns of one color on a single file: doubled pawns.
This move is fatal. The other side can now drive the king into a forced mate. Trace the attack back to the moment the defense gave way.
A forced checkmate was on the board, and this move lets it go. When the king is trapped, finish the job. Go back and find the mate.
A sacrifice with real substance. Take the material, and in the checked line the sacrifice still stands. That takes nerve and calculation.
Exact defense. Of every move checked, only this one kept the position playable; the others were losing. Remember that defense.
Only this move kept hold of the advantage. Every alternative that was checked lost. Everything rested on that one move.
The reply is an immediate capture. Something is left to be taken, and it should have been seen before moving.
Check is the strongest reply. The king must be answered first, and that check belongs in every calculation.
This is not the best. The engine prefers another move, and its replies tell a different story. Set the two side by side.
This move falls short of the engine's best. The reply shows where the value leaks away. Locate it.
Strong, and solid. Among the moves the engine examined, this one gives up almost nothing. Little else came close.
Sound, though not the best. The engine prefers another move, yet the bulk of the position's value is kept.
The clock was nearly spent when this move was made. Pressure like that tests everything.
Fast, with time to spare. Speed is only worth it when the move is right.
The clock shows heavy thinking before this move. Time is a resource; spend it where the position demands it.
Theory recognizes this move. A name says where the game is, not what to play.
Theory runs out at this move. From here, judgment has to replace memory.
After the earlier setback, this move puts the position back on its feet. That is fighting back, and it counts.
The earlier setback is undone, and the game is alive again. The opponent's errors played a part. Take the gift, but do not rely on it.
An error by the opponent on the last move, and this one makes them pay. Errors are there to be punished.
The opponent's last move was an error, and it goes unpunished. When the other side errs, make them pay.
This same issue has already appeared in this game. An issue that keeps returning is a habit forming. Compare the moments and name the warning sign.
The piece left hanging earlier is guarded once more. Keep it that way.
There was no one blunder here. Concession after small concession has drained the position, and this move adds another. Little leaks sink positions.
Through every reviewed move, the advantage stayed in hand until the win. Converting cleanly is a skill, and this was done well.
The saved games show this same issue more than once. It is a pattern now, and patterns must be broken. Study those games beside this one.
It is checkmate; every escape for the king is closed. The attack is complete.
It is checkmate, with every escape for the king closed. The defense failed earlier; go back and find where it could have held.
A draw. The result stands, yet the decisions that led here still deserve a hard look.
Study the position. When you are sure, commit to your move.
Not good enough yet. Look again, and calculate more carefully.
That attempt produced nothing to judge. Make your move again, and it will be checked.
The saved engine analysis finds a forced checkmate for the side that made this move.
The saved engine analysis gives the other side a forced checkmate once this move is made.
Count the material at the end of the saved line: the side that made this move is ahead of where it began.
Count the material at the end of the saved line: the side that made this move is behind where it began.
The move is accepted here. No clear tactical reason comes out of the moves shown, and I will not invent one.
The move is rejected here. No clear tactical reason comes out of the moves shown, and I will not pretend otherwise.
The move matches one of this exercise's saved answers. Here, the saved answers set the standard.
The saved answers for this exercise do not include this move. Another legal move can still be good chess; this one simply falls outside what the exercise accepts.
Study this move until you understand it. Then take on the next position.
A good move, then. Know why it works, not just that it does.
Practice saved for the record. Your review schedule is left as it was.
Solved, but this recall remains flagged for relearning. One success is not mastery.
This is where it begins, before a single move of the line. Take the position in fully.
The next move is on the board. See exactly what it changes.
A check. The king is attacked, and everything else waits until that is answered.
With this move, the king steps out of check.
Promotion. The pawn has crossed the whole board and is a pawn no longer.
Promotion with check: the pawn becomes a new piece on the last rank, and the enemy king is attacked.
The pawn promotes on the last rank, and it is checkmate. The king is out of squares.
Promotion, and with it the king is released from check.
A plain capture, nothing more.
This move captures a piece and gives check in the same stroke.
A capture, and it is checkmate. There is no way out for the king.
This move captures a piece, and the capture takes the king out of check.
The pawn takes a piece as it steps onto the last rank, then promotes.
The pawn captures, promotes on the last rank, and gives check, all in one move.
Capture, promotion and checkmate, all from one pawn move. No legal escape remains.
The pawn captures its way to promotion, and that move also frees its king from check.
The king castles, the rook comes across, and the same move delivers check.
The king castles, the rook comes across, and it is checkmate. Nothing can save the opposing king.
This is a fork that pays. One piece attacks several targets, then takes one, and this example ends with a net material gain.
The marked capture is off limits, because that piece is pinned against its king. Leaving would uncover the king behind it, which the rules forbid.
The piece under attack is pinned in front of its king. Its escape is limited to moves that keep the king covered, and that narrows the defense.
The capture stands: each defender is pinned to its king, so none of them can take back. Material is gained in the line shown.
The pinned piece is chained to its line by the king behind it. It is held there, and as these moves play out, it is captured.
The front piece gives way, and the piece behind it falls along the same line. That is the skewer doing its work.
The check forces the king aside. Then that attacker collects the piece the king was shielding.
The defender falls first, and it was the only one. Then, later in these moves, the piece it guarded falls too. Remove the guard, then take the prize.
The defender is dragged off its duty, and the piece it had to guard goes next.
The blocking piece moves, and a capture comes along the line it opened, made by the piece behind.
Check comes from behind: the front piece moves, and the hidden piece strikes the king.
A double check. The king is attacked by two pieces at once, and nothing but a king move can meet it.
One move, two attackers: the moving piece strikes, and the line it vacates lets another strike too. Here, the second attacker takes its target.
Promotion, and in this example the promoting side comes out ahead in material.
The piece had no defender, and it is captured. In this example, the capture leaves that side ahead in material.
With its previous move, the opponent released a relative pin on the attacking piece. The target never moved, and it is captured in the line shown.
The other side has the marked reply available, and it is legal. Play it, and see what it does to the position.
Before every move, find any piece of yours that could be captured without a useful recapture.
No quiet move until every unguarded enemy piece has been counted.
Search the forcing moves for one piece that attacks two valuable targets at once.
A pinned piece shields what stands behind it, the king or something more valuable. Know which before you move it.
An attack does not stop at the first target. Check the line behind it for something more valuable.
Trade a defender, and its protection leaves with it. Learn its duties before you trade it.
A blocking piece that moves opens lines behind it. Know where every one of them leads.
Search the position for a single move with two threats. Checks count, and so do lines that a move opens.
Before a back-rank defender moves, check that the king still has an escape square.
Count a pawn's distance to promotion in moves, then calculate every forcing pawn advance.
A defender has duties. Name them all before it moves. Each of those pieces loses that protection when it goes.
Judge an exchange by its last capture, not its first. Add up every piece that changes hands.
Check whether a forcing exchange can drag a defender away from another target it guards.
The saved answers are the standard here. Other legal moves may be perfectly good chess; they simply are not what this exercise asks for.
The moves shown are played against strong replies. Strong is not the same as forced, so do not treat every reply here as the only one.
Material is counted for the line shown only, against where that line began. The written explanation spells out the values used.
No simple tactical reason comes out of the saved line. Go through it move by move and judge each reply yourself, and do not read a positional reason into it.
What this explanation accepts is set by the exercise's saved answer policy. Look to the written notes for the setting.
This is the line you are studying, move by move. Learn these moves well enough to play them without help.
Right. That move is part of the material you chose to study.
The answer lies in the study lines you selected. Play a move from them.
Your selected opening lines allow several moves here. Play any one of them.
Your selected study material holds the move for this position. Bring it back from memory.
That move is not in the opening lines you selected to study. Make another attempt.
Wrong for the opening lines you selected. Make another attempt. Because the study changed, its review schedule ignores this saved attempt.
That move lies outside the opening lines you selected. Attempt it again. The position is retired; its schedule will not move.
Any move from this line counts in mixed Due. Dedicated practice demands this line alone.
Recalls on the schedule test the side you selected. Studies that reach the same position share a single card.
First reload the saved session. Your next move comes after that.
Watch every move of the verified line as the board replays it.
The solution was revealed, and the attempt is saved that way. Replay the solution below, and learn it properly.
Solved, at the second attempt. The miss and the solve both go on your record. Next time, find it first.
Every move correct, start to finish. That is how a puzzle should be solved.
That does not solve it. What you got right before it is kept.
Right so far. The puzzle is not finished; find the next move.
Calculate before you move. A puzzle rewards precision, not haste.
The engine gives me too little to explain this position, and I will not guess.
Your review is on pause. Pick it up again below, or test a move of your own on the board.
Choose a move to review, or play a different one on the board to test it.
This move stands in established opening theory.
Theory knows this move. It is part of a recognized opening.
Theory recognizes this as an opening move. Theory can name it; it cannot play the position.
Theory still holds here.
Another established move.
The answer is theory too.
The known lines carry on.
Theory still covers this.
The established line runs on.
Theory has not run out yet.
One more move theory already knows. Knowing a line and understanding it are not the same.
Your game awaits judgment. Go through it, and we will see which moves earned their place.
Not the move this lesson calls for, though the rules allow it. Again.
Correct. The lesson asked for exactly that.
Shown, this time. Learn it, so it need not be shown again.
Observe the line closely. Every move in it matters.
Now, from memory and without help, play the studied line.
A side line. Master it, then return.
Chapter complete, and recorded.
Every move of the game is now before you. Go through it with care.
The lesson must be reloaded. Nothing goes forward until then.
